name: How long antidepressants take to work
headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. The NHS says sertraline can be used for depression and for other conditions, including obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and social anxiety disorder. The NHS says most adults can take sertraline, but it is not suitable for everyone, for example some people with heart problems, glaucoma or epilepsy.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include headaches, feeling or being sick, sweating and a dry mouth. The NHS says most of these side effects are mild and ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer.

The NHS also says that some people feel worse during the first few weeks of citalopram before they begin to feel better. Sexual side effects are a separate matter, because the NHS says they can sometimes be long lasting and may not get better even after the medicine is stopped. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

Questions about side effects can go to a pharmacist or GP. The NHS says to call NHS 111 for a serious side effect or for thoughts of self-harm. A serious allergic reaction, called anaphylaxis, is rare, and the NHS says to call 999 if it may be happening.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says to talk to the doctor if citalopram has not helped after 6 weeks. More generally, the NHS says that if an antidepressant brings no benefit after about 4 weeks, a GP or mental health specialist can be asked about options. These options can include trying a different medicine.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says that if the person and doctor decide to stop it, the doctor will recommend reducing the dose gradually to help prevent withdrawal side effects.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects. It says the speed of reduction is agreed between the person and their healthcare professional, who reviews them during the reduction. NICE also says that missed doses or taking less than a full dose can cause withdrawal symptoms. Clinicians are asked to explain that withdrawal symptoms are not the same as the depression coming back. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back. The NHS 111 Wales site says withdrawal symptoms can be severe for some people and can last a lot longer.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline taken for depression, the NHS says treatment usually continues for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. Some people with recurrent depression may be advised to continue for much longer.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, people registered with a GP can usually refer themselves for free NHS talking therapies.
